# Food Safety Report

## Emek Gilboa Yellow Cheese, 22% Fat, 200 g — Tnuva

---

## 1. Overall verdict

This cheese contains one additive, potassium sorbate (E202), a preservative that European food safety assessments consider acceptable at current levels of consumption but that carries some open questions. Nothing here points to an immediate concern, but E202 is classified as **controversial** rather than fully unproblematic.

---

## 2. The additive in detail

### E202 — Potassium sorbate
**Classification: Controversial**

Potassium sorbate is a preservative used to keep food from spoiling. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) has found no evidence that it causes cancer and no evidence that it damages genetic material, and current consumption levels are judged to stay below the safe daily limit ([EFSA 2015](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4144); [EFSA/FAF 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009143/)).

However, three things justify a cautious rating rather than a plain "OK":

- **The safe daily limit has been lowered.** The long-standing acceptable daily intake of 25 mg per kg of body weight per day was replaced in 2015 by a temporary limit of just 3 mg, and then set in 2019 at 11 mg — still well under the original figure. The reason was findings on reproduction and development in animal studies ([EFSA 2015](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4144); [EFSA/FAF 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009143/)).

- **What those animal studies showed.** At high doses, studies reported effects on offspring (including delayed physical and functional development and reduced litter weight), reduced weights of female reproductive organs, lower body weight gain in both parents and pups, and raised blood cholesterol. These effects appeared only at very high doses, far above what people consume, and safety margins were built in accordingly — but they were considered significant enough to force the limit to be revised ([EFSA 2015](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4144); [EFSA/FAF 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009143/)).

- **An unresolved question about mixtures.** In laboratory tests, substances formed when sorbic acid reacts with nitrites, or with vitamin C in the presence of iron salts, showed the ability to damage genetic material. These ingredient combinations are allowed together in some food categories (such as olives and food supplements). EFSA noted that no study has looked at what happens in real foods during processing and storage, and an industry report submitted in 2019 added no new information — so this gap remains open ([EFSA 2015](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4144); [EFSA/FAF 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009143/)).

One further point worth knowing: in the 2015 review, the temporary daily limit was exceeded only among toddlers and children in one country at the highest consumption levels. Under the current 2019 limit, EFSA concluded it would not be exceeded in the standard exposure scenario ([EFSA 2015](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4144); [EFSA/FAF 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009143/)).

---

## 3. Additives with insufficient data

None. The single additive identified in this product has been evaluated and classified.

---

*This report summarises existing published safety assessments and adds no information beyond them.*

# Food Safety Report

**Product:** Naama Processed Cheese with Mushrooms, 25% Fat, 240 g
**Brand:** Tnuva

---

## Overall verdict

This processed cheese contains three additives that regulators consider debated (two phosphate-based emulsifiers and one preservative), plus one additive for which the available documentation did not allow any assessment. None of the additives reviewed here is described in the sources as a proven hazard, but the phosphates and the preservative each come with cautions worth knowing about.

---

## Additive-by-additive review

### E450 — Diphosphates
**Classification: Controversial**

European food safety authorities (EFSA, 2019) set a maximum recommended daily intake for phosphates, expressed as phosphorus, of 40 mg per kilogram of body weight per day, and concluded this level is protective for the general population. The experts found phosphates to have low short-term toxicity, no concern regarding effects on genes or cancer, and no effects in studies on development. The caution comes from how much people actually consume: the panel found that estimated intakes go above this recommended limit for infants, toddlers and other children on average, and for infants, toddlers, children and adolescents among the highest consumers, as well as through food supplements. The panel also stated that this recommended limit does not apply to people with moderate to severe kidney impairment. It further noted that very high phosphorus intakes may upset the body's regulation of phosphorus, calcium and vitamin D, which could contribute to bone loss, while stressing that the evidence linking dietary phosphates to heart problems or to reduced bone density remains insufficient and inconsistent. ([EFSA, 2019](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2019.5674))

### E452 — Polyphosphates
**Classification: Controversial**

E452 was assessed by EFSA in the same 2019 review as E450 and shares the same recommended limit of 40 mg phosphorus per kilogram of body weight per day. As with E450, the experts reported low short-term toxicity, no concern for effects on genes or cancer, and no effects on development. The same cautions apply: estimated intakes exceed the recommended limit for infants, toddlers and other children on average and for young people among the highest consumers, and food supplements can push intakes above the limit too. The limit does not apply to people with moderate to severe kidney impairment. The panel noted possible disruption of phosphorus, calcium and vitamin D regulation at very high intakes, with a possible contribution to bone loss, but repeatedly described the evidence on heart outcomes and fractures as insufficient and confounded, and called for better intake data. ([EFSA, 2019](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2019.5674))

### E330 — Citric acid
**Classification: Insufficient data**

We cannot give an assessment of this additive. The document available to us does not evaluate E330 as a food additive at all: it is a safety review of a different family of additives (E472a–f, the esters of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids). Citric acid appears in that document only as a chemical component of one of those other additives, never as the subject of a safety evaluation. No toxicological data, intake estimate, safe-intake limit or conclusion specific to E330 was available, so no conclusion — reassuring or otherwise — can be drawn here. ([EFSA opinion on E472a–f](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7448088/))

### E202 — Potassium sorbate (preservative)
**Classification: Controversial**

Potassium sorbate is not classified as cancer-causing, and the assessments found no evidence that it damages genes; current estimated intakes are judged to stay below the recommended safe limit. However, that limit has been lowered over time: the older recommendation of 25 mg per kilogram of body weight per day was cut in 2015 to a temporary 3 mg, then set in 2019 at 11 mg — still well below the original figure. The reason was findings in animal reproduction and development studies at very high doses, including changes in male pups, delayed physical and functional development, reduced organ weights in females, lower weight gain and raised blood cholesterol. Experts also flagged an unresolved question: substances formed when sorbic acid reacts with nitrites, or with vitamin C in the presence of iron salts, were shown to cause genetic changes in laboratory tests, and no study exists on what forms in real foods during processing and storage; an industry report submitted in 2019 added no new information. Finally, the 2015 review noted that the temporary limit was exceeded by high-consuming toddlers and children in one country. ([EFSA, 2015](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4144); [EFSA, 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009143/))

# Food Safety Report — Tnuva Cottage Cheese 1% Fat 250g (Tnuva)

## Overall verdict

This product contains one additive of note — phosphates — which is classified as **controversial**: European food safety authorities have not identified a proven hazard at normal levels of use, but they have flagged that some population groups already take in more phosphates than the recommended daily limit from all sources combined.

---

## Additive by additive

### Phosphates — *Controversial*

Phosphates are widely used food additives. In its review, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) set a "group acceptable daily intake" (ADI) of 40 mg of phosphorus per kilogram of body weight per day, and concluded that this level is protective for the general population. The Panel also reported that phosphates have low acute toxicity when swallowed, raised no concern regarding genotoxicity or cancer, and produced no effects in developmental toxicity studies. ([EFSA, 2019](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2019.5674))

The reason for caution is not the additive itself in a single food, but total intake across the diet. EFSA's exposure estimates exceeded the recommended daily limit for infants, toddlers and other children at average intake levels, and for infants, toddlers, children and adolescents at the high (95th percentile) intake level. The Panel also noted that intake of phosphates from food supplements exceeds the proposed limit. ([EFSA, 2019](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2019.5674))

EFSA further specified that this daily limit does **not** apply to people with moderate to severe reduced kidney function, because the safety margin used only covers people with slight kidney impairment. People in that situation may wish to discuss phosphate intake with their doctor. ([EFSA, 2019](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2019.5674))

Finally, the scientific picture on long-term health effects is not settled. EFSA stated that there is insufficient evidence to link dietary phosphate intake to cardiovascular outcomes, while noting some evidence linking phosphorus levels measured in blood to cardiovascular disease and cardiovascular mortality. Findings on bone health were inconsistent between studies (one study showed an effect only in women, another only in men). Separately, the Panel concluded that the available data did not raise safety concerns for infants under 16 weeks of age consuming formula or food for medical purposes. ([EFSA, 2019](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2019.5674))

**In plain terms:** phosphates are not classified as something to avoid, and no proven harm has been demonstrated at ordinary levels of consumption. The caution comes from the fact that overall intake from the whole diet can exceed the recommended limit, particularly in children, and that the limit does not cover people with significant kidney problems.

---

*This report is based solely on the classifications and evidence provided; no additional health information has been added.*

# Food Safety Report

## Yoplait Diet with Citrus Fruits, 150 g — Tnuva

---

## Overall verdict

This yogurt contains three additives: two of them (the modified starch E1442 and the sweetener acesulfame K) are considered safe by food safety authorities at the levels used in food. The third, aspartame, is judged safe for the general population at current intake levels, but carries specific caveats — notably that it is not suitable for people with phenylketonuria (PKU) — which is why we classify it as controversial.

---

## Additive-by-additive review

### E1442 — Hydroxypropyl starch phosphate (thickener)
**Classification: OK**

E1442 is a modified starch used to give the yogurt its texture. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) re-examined modified starches and concluded there is no safety concern at the amounts used in food, and that no maximum daily intake figure needs to be set. The reason is simple: this starch is not absorbed as-is by the body — it is broken down in the gut like other starches. Long-term animal studies at very high doses showed no effects relevant to human health, and no genotoxic concern was identified.

One point for transparency: EFSA did recommend tightening the allowed limits for trace metal impurities (arsenic, lead, mercury) in modified starches. This is a purity/manufacturing quality issue, not a problem with the additive itself. EFSA also flagged a data gap for infants and young children consuming special medical foods — but that gap concerns other modified starches, **not** E1442.
*(Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009865/pdf/EFS2-15-e04911.pdf)*

---

### Aspartame (E951) — sweetener
**Classification: Controversial**

EFSA's 2013 review concluded that aspartame is not a safety concern at current consumption levels, or at the acceptable daily intake of 40 mg per kg of body weight per day — and the authority saw no reason to lower that figure. Long-term animal studies did not show an increase in tumours, and the overall evidence did not point to a genotoxic concern (though one study reported an "equivocal" positive result in female mice).

So why "controversial" rather than "OK"? Because EFSA itself attached several caveats. First and most clearly: **the acceptable daily intake does not apply to people with phenylketonuria (PKU)**, an inherited condition. People who carry one copy of the PKU gene also have a narrower safety margin than the general population. Second, EFSA stated that developmental effects at doses lower than those tested in animals "could not be excluded," and acknowledged uncertainties in the available data on how aspartame behaves in the body. These are open questions rather than proven risks for the general public — hence the cautious classification. No cancer agency classification is mentioned in the source used here.
*(Source: https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2013.3496)*

---

### Acesulfame K (E950) — sweetener
**Classification: OK**

EFSA re-evaluated acesulfame K in 2025 and concluded there is no safety concern at the levels used in food. Notably, the authority *raised* the acceptable daily intake to 15 mg per kg of body weight per day (up from the previous 9 mg), which is the opposite of a precautionary tightening. Estimated intakes across the population — including among the highest consumers — were generally below that level. No genotoxicity concern was found for acesulfame K or its breakdown products.

One caveat concerns manufacturing quality rather than the sweetener itself: a possible impurity (5-chloro-acesulfame) raised a computer-modelled genotoxicity alert, so EFSA recommended setting a strict limit on it or requesting further data.
*(Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12041894/)*

---

## Note on data gaps

None of the three additives in this product fell into the "insufficient data" category. All three had enough evidence available for the authorities to reach a conclusion.

# Food Safety Report — Jelly Pineapple Flavor 125 g EDCH (Tnuva)

## Overall verdict

This product contains one additive that we have flagged as **controversial**: carrageenan (E 407). European food safety authorities did not identify a proven hazard from food-grade carrageenan, but they also left several questions open, which is why it is not simply rated "OK".

---

## Additive by additive

### Carrageenan (E 407) — **Controversial**

Carrageenan is a thickening/gelling ingredient obtained from seaweed. In its 2018 re-evaluation, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) found no concern regarding cancer risk or damage to genetic material, and noted that the substance is not absorbed into the body in its intact form; no adverse effects were seen in animal studies even at very high doses ([EFSA 2018](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5238)). However, EFSA said the acceptable daily intake of 75 mg per kg of body weight should be considered only **temporary**, because it identified uncertainties about the additive's chemistry, about how much people actually consume, and about the biological and toxicological data; it asked for a better set of data within five years ([EFSA 2018](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5238)). EFSA was also able to make a refined consumption estimate for only 41 of 79 food categories, and in a "brand-loyal" scenario (someone always eating the same brands) intake for toddlers could reach up to 758.6 mg per kg of body weight per day — well above the temporary acceptable daily intake ([EFSA 2018](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5238)).

EFSA's re-evaluation concluded there is no safety concern at the reported uses and use levels, and that no numerical daily limit (ADI) is needed. The body does not absorb it as-is: it is broken down in the gut and fermented, producing end products that EFSA states do not raise any safety concern. Long-term animal studies at very high intakes showed no effects relevant to human risk, and no genetic-damage concern was identified ([EFSA opinion](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009865/pdf/EFS2-15-e04911.pdf)).

One point of context: EFSA did note a data gap for infants and young children consuming special medical foods, but that gap applies to other modified starches (such as E1450), not to E1442. The only recommendation concerning E1442 was to tighten the allowed limits for trace metal impurities (arsenic, lead, mercury) — a purity/manufacturing standard, not a property of the additive itself ([same source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009865/pdf/EFS2-15-e04911.pdf)).

---

### Aspartame — Sweetener (E951)
**Classification: Controversial**

EFSA's 2013 re-evaluation concluded that aspartame is **not** of safety concern at current exposure estimates or at its acceptable daily intake (ADI) of 40 mg per kg of body weight per day, and the panel saw no reason to lower that limit. Long-term animal studies did not show an increase in tumours, and the overall weight of evidence did not indicate a concern for genetic damage ([EFSA opinion](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2013.3496)).

It is nonetheless classified as controversial rather than simply "OK" for three reasons stated by EFSA itself. First, the panel explicitly says the ADI **does not apply to people with phenylketonuria (PKU)**, a genetic condition; people who carry one copy of the PKU gene also have a narrower safety margin than the general population. Second, the panel could not rule out the possibility of developmental effects in animals at doses below the level it tested as safe, and pointed to remaining uncertainties in the available human and animal data. Third, one study reported an "equivocal positive" genetic-damage result in one group of specially bred female mice, although the overall conclusion across all studies was negative ([EFSA opinion](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2013.3496)).

---

### Acesulfame K — Sweetener (E950)
**Classification: OK**

EFSA's 2025 re-evaluation states plainly that there is no safety concern at the reported uses and use levels. Notably, the panel **raised** the acceptable daily intake to 15 mg per kg of body weight per day (up from the previous 9 mg), which is the opposite of a precautionary tightening. Estimated intakes, including among the highest consumers, were generally below this limit across all population groups ([EFSA re-evaluation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12041894/)).

No concern for genetic damage was found for acesulfame K or its breakdown products, and no cancer classification is mentioned. The only caution raised concerns a possible manufacturing impurity (5-chloro-acesulfame), for which EFSA recommended either a strict maximum limit or additional data — again a question of production purity rather than the sweetener itself ([same source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12041894/)).

None of the three additives reviewed here falls into the "insufficient data" category — each has been formally evaluated by EFSA with conclusions available. Where uncertainties remain (the limited data behind some aspartame conclusions, and the impurity questions for E1442 and acesulfame K), these are described above as the sources state them.

To be clear: **this is not a warning and not a clean bill of health** — it simply means the evidence needed to classify E500 is missing here (https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5209).

---

## E471 — Mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids — Controversial

**Classification: controversial**

**Why it is not a concern in itself:** Once swallowed, E471 is broken down in the digestive system into glycerol and fatty acids — two substances that European experts have themselves reviewed and considered of no safety concern. Animal studies (short-term, long-term, and on reproduction and development) showed no harmful effects, and no cancer-causing or DNA-damaging potential was identified. EFSA concluded in 2017 that no maximum daily intake figure was needed and that E471 was "of no safety concern at the reported uses and use levels", including for infants under 16 weeks (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7010209/).

**Why it is nevertheless flagged as controversial:** In a 2021 re-examination, EFSA looked at the *impurities* that can be present in E471 (rather than the additive itself). It found that estimated intakes exceeded the reference values for a substance called 3-MCPD in infants under 16 weeks, and for glycidyl esters and erucic acid across all age groups. The panel called for the current limits on arsenic, lead, cadmium and mercury in E471 to be lowered, and for new limits to be set for these impurities (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8573540/).

**A remaining knowledge gap:** EFSA also noted that studies on other emulsifiers have shown effects on gut bacteria, and that this "might also be relevant to emulsifiers in general" — but no specific study exists on E471 and gut bacteria. This is an acknowledged gap, not a demonstrated effect (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8573540/).

---

## E407 — Carrageenan — Controversial

**Classification: controversial**

**Why it is not classed as "avoid":** Food-grade carrageenan did not raise concerns about DNA damage or cancer in EFSA's review, and animal studies showed no adverse effects even at the highest doses tested (https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5238).

**Why it is flagged as controversial:** EFSA explicitly listed uncertainties about the chemistry of the additive, about how much people actually consume, and about the biological data. As a result, the existing acceptable daily intake of 75 mg per kg of body weight was made only **temporary**, with a request for the evidence base to be improved within five years. In addition, estimated intakes for toddlers who regularly consume the same brands reached up to roughly ten times that temporary daily figure. Results between studies were also inconsistent, with one long-term rat study pointing to effects at a much lower dose than others (https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5238).

**One further point:** EFSA was informed by an interested party that carrageenan on the market does not necessarily meet EU specifications regarding its low molecular weight fraction. That fraction resembles "degraded carrageenan", a different substance which is **not authorised as a food additive** and which caused intestinal damage and tumours in rats and intestinal lesions and anaemia in monkeys. This concerns the unauthorised degraded form, not food-grade carrageenan itself (https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5238).

# Food Safety Report

**Product:** Danone PRO Lemon Cream Flavor — No Added Sugar, 20 g Protein, 0% Fat (brand: Strauss)

---

## Overall verdict

This product contains three additives: two of them (modified starch E1442 and acesulfame K) are considered safe by European food safety authorities at the levels used in food. The third, sucralose, is also considered safe at current authorised uses, but experts have flagged one unresolved question about what happens to it at high cooking temperatures — so we class it as "controversial" rather than fully "OK".

---

## Additive by additive

### E1442 — Hydroxypropyl starch phosphate (modified starch)
**Classification: OK**

This is a starch that has been chemically modified so it thickens and stabilises food. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) reviewed modified starches and concluded there is no safety concern at the amounts used in food — so much so that no maximum daily intake figure was considered necessary. The reason is that these starches are not absorbed as such by the body: they are broken down in the gut and fermented, producing substances that raise no safety concern. Long-term animal studies at very high doses showed no effects relevant to human health, and no concern about damage to DNA was identified. ([EFSA re-evaluation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009865/pdf/EFS2-15-e04911.pdf))

One point of context: EFSA did note a data gap for infants and young children who consume special medical foods, but that gap concerns *other* modified starches (such as E1450), not E1442. The only remark specifically touching E1442 was a technical request to tighten the allowed limits for trace metal impurities (arsenic, lead, mercury) — a purity/manufacturing quality issue, not a problem with the additive itself.

---

### Acesulfame K (E950) — sweetener
**Classification: OK**

Acesulfame K is a calorie-free sweetener. EFSA re-evaluated it in 2025 and stated plainly that there is no safety concern at the reported uses and levels. The experts set an acceptable daily intake of 15 mg per kg of body weight per day — notably, this is *higher* than the previous limit of 9 mg/kg, meaning the review made the assessment less restrictive, not more. Estimated intakes, even among the highest consumers (95th percentile), were generally below that limit in all population groups. No concern was found regarding DNA damage, either for the sweetener or its breakdown products. ([EFSA 2025 re-evaluation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12041894/))

The single caution raised concerns a possible manufacturing impurity (5-chloro-acesulfame), for which EFSA recommended setting a strict maximum limit or obtaining more data. Again, this is about production purity standards, not about the sweetener as normally used.

---

### Sucralose (E955) — sweetener
**Classification: Controversial**

For the uses currently allowed in Europe — which includes products like this one — EFSA's conclusion is reassuring. The Panel kept the acceptable daily intake at 15 mg per kg of body weight per day, and found that estimated intakes, including for high consumers, stay below that level in all population groups. No concern was identified regarding DNA damage from sucralose or its impurities. EFSA also examined and rejected a study (Ramazzini Institute) that had suggested sucralose caused blood-related tumours in male mice, noting there was no dose–response relationship and no such effect in adequate studies in rats and mice. ([EFSA 2017 statement](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7010144/), [EFSA opinion](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12911467/))

Why "controversial" then? Because EFSA itself left one question open. When asked whether sucralose could be extended to fine bakery products, the Panel said it **could not reach a conclusion**, because of uncertainty about whether chlorinated compounds might form when sucralose is exposed to the wide range of baking conditions. It also recommended that authorities look into possible unwanted breakdown products when people cook at home at high temperatures, such as frying or baking. Nothing harmful has been demonstrated — this is an acknowledged gap in knowledge, not a proven risk. EFSA additionally recommended tightening the purity specifications (specific limits for two impurities, 4-CG and 1,6-DCF, and a lower lead limit). ([EFSA opinion](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12911467/))

Since this product is a chilled dairy-type product, not a baked one, the high-temperature question does not directly apply to how it is consumed.

---

## Note on data gaps

None of the three additives in this product falls into the "insufficient data" category. Where uncertainties exist, they have been described above and attributed to the source that raised them.

## Overall verdict

This spread contains three additives: one considered safe by European regulators, one that carries some open questions, and one for which we simply don't have assessment data on hand. Nothing in the available evidence points to a proven hazard at normal use levels, but one additive (E200) deserves a nuanced look.

---

## Additive by additive

### E1442 — Hydroxypropyl starch phosphate
**Classification: OK**

This is a modified starch used to give texture and thickness. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) reviewed modified starches of this type and concluded there is no safety concern at the levels used in food, to the point that no maximum daily intake figure was considered necessary. The reason is straightforward: the body doesn't absorb this starch as-is — it is broken down in the digestive system and fermented by gut bacteria, producing substances that raise no concern. Long-term animal studies at very high doses showed no effects relevant to human health, and no concern was identified regarding effects on DNA.

One point worth noting for transparency: EFSA recommended tightening the purity limits for trace metals (arsenic, lead, mercury) in the manufacturing specifications. This is a manufacturing-quality issue, not a problem with the additive itself. A separate data gap flagged by EFSA — concerning infants and young children using special medical foods — applies to other modified starches, not to E1442.
(Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009865/pdf/EFS2-15-e04911.pdf)

---

### E200 — Sorbic acid
**Classification: Controversial**

Sorbic acid is a preservative used to prevent mould and yeast growth. EFSA has not identified a proven hazard at authorised levels: no effect on DNA was found for sorbic acid or potassium sorbate, no cancer-causing effect was seen in long-term animal studies, and in 2019 EFSA set an acceptable daily intake of 11 mg per kg of body weight, concluding that people's actual intake would not exceed it.

So why "controversial"? Because the acceptable daily limit has been revised downward significantly over time — from 25 mg/kg in 1996, down to a temporary 3 mg/kg in 2015, then settled at 11 mg/kg in 2019. The reason for that revision was findings in rat studies concerning reproduction and development: reduced anogenital distance in male second-generation pups, delays in physical and functional development, lower ovary and uterus weights and increased blood cholesterol at high doses. In the 2015 assessment, the temporary limit was exceeded by toddlers and children in one country.

EFSA also flagged an unresolved question: sorbic acid can react with nitrites, or with vitamin C in the presence of iron, to form substances shown to affect DNA in laboratory tests — and no study has yet examined whether this happens in real foods during processing and storage. Separately, calcium sorbate (E203, a different additive) was excluded from the shared daily limit for lack of data; this does not apply to E200 itself.
(Sources: https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4144, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7009143/)

---

### E385 — Calcium disodium EDTA
**Classification: Insufficient data**

We have no EFSA assessment on file for this additive. This means we cannot say whether it is safe, problematic, or anything in between — the absence of data here is a gap in our information, not evidence of either safety or risk. Anyone wanting a conclusion on E385 will need to consult a source with a completed evaluation.
(Source: none available)
